saa-avc-194.text: A company with support AWS Business is a fast and automated way to identify common cost optimization opportunities in your account — such as idle/unused load balancers (zero requests for a long period), volumes EBS not attached, for instance EC2 with use of CPU very low in recent 2 weeks, and clusters Redshift underutilized — without building custom scripts, as a starting point before investing in more advanced tools (such as Computer Optimizer for deeper analysis of EC2).
options: Use conformance packs from AWS Configure to evaluate cost-related configuration rules
Configure the AWS Cost Anomaly Detection to identify underutilized resources
Enable AWS CloudTrail and analyze patterns of calls from API to identify unused resources
Use the 'Cost Optimization' category checks AWS Trusted Advisor (available in Business or Enterprise support plans)
saa-avc-194.explanation: Correct. Cost Optimization checks of the Trusted Advisor include 'Idle Load Balancers'' (ALB/CLB/NLB without any requests by 7 days), 'Underutilized' Amazon EBS Volumes' (not attached or with very low activity), 'Low Use Amazon EC2 Mechanisms' (CPU less than one limit per 14 days), and verifications of 'Amazon Redshift Reserved Node Optimization'/use, among others — providing fast, automated and unconfigured analysis of common cost optimization opportunities across the account.
saa-avc-194.hint: Think of what tool the AWS already comes with ready checks, categorized as 'cost optimization', that signal idle or underutilized resources without additional configuration.
optionRationales: Correct. Cost Optimization checks of the Trusted Advisor include 'Idle Load Balancers'' (ALB/CLB/NLB without any requests by 7 days), 'Underutilized' Amazon EBS Volumes' (not attached or with very low activity), 'Low Use Amazon EC2 Mechanisms' (CPU less than one limit per 14 days), and verifications of 'Amazon Redshift Reserved Node Optimization'/use, among others — providing fast, automated and unconfigured analysis of common cost optimization opportunities across the account.

Incorrect. The conformance packs of AWS Config are designed to evaluate rules of COMPLIANCE/CONFIGURATION (e.g. 'encryption is enabled', 'the required tags are present') — although some config rules may be cost-related, this is not the mechanism specifically designed to identify idle/underutilized resources for cost optimization, and would require building custom rules — more effort than integrated verifications of the Trusted Advisor.

Incorrect. Cost Anomaly Detection identifies FATHER PARENTS GASTO INCOMUNS in comparison to historical baselines (e.g., a sudden peak of cost) — does not identify resources ESTRUTURALMENTE idle/underused (as a volume) EBS that SEMPRE it was not attached, which would not appear as an 'anomaly' expenditure since its cost pattern is consistent) — the verifications of the Trusted Advisor specifically aimed at this type of persistent underuse.

Incorrect. Analyze logs of CloudTrail for calling patterns of API in order to infer the use of resources would require significant analysis/customized tools of logs, and the CloudTrail mainly records CHAMADAS OF API (management plan), not necessarily continuous METRICS as use of CPU or counting of requests for load balancer necessary to identify ' idle'/'underused' resources — or Trusted Advisor provides these specific checks ready for use.

saa-avc-195.text: A company has dozens of functions Lambda and services ECS that send logs to the Amazon CloudWatch Logs. By default, log groups created automatically (e.g. by Lambda) they have a retention defined as 'Never Expire', which means that log data accumulate indefinitely. Over time, this resulted in terabytes of old logs rarely accessed, contributing significantly to the storage bill of the CloudWatch Logs. The team wants to reduce the continuous storage costs of these logs, keeping recent history sufficient for debugging (ex.: 30-90 days), without excluding manually logs.
options: Export logs from CloudWatch Logs for the Amazon S3 and delete the original log groups
Migration from CloudWatch Logs for the Amazon OpenSearch Service for log storage
Configure log retention policies in log groups CloudWatch Logs, defining an appropriate retention period (ex.: 30 or 90 days) instead of 'Never Expire''
Reduce the log level of applications (e.g. DEBUG for ERROR) to generate less logs
saa-avc-195.explanation: Correct. The retention settings of the CloudWatch Logs automatically and permanently delete log events older than the configured retention period, directly reducing the volume of stored log data (and associated storage costs) over time, while retaining a defined window of recent logs for debugging — this can be configured by log group (manually, via CLI/IAC, or in mass, saw a script that iterated on the log groups).
saa-avc-195.hint: Think about what native configuration of the log groups of CloudWatch Logs automatically deletes log events older than a defined period, without manual exclusion.
optionRationales: Correct. The retention settings of the CloudWatch Logs automatically and permanently delete log events older than the configured retention period, directly reducing the volume of stored log data (and associated storage costs) over time, while retaining a defined window of recent logs for debugging — this can be configured by log group (manually, via CLI/IAC, or in mass, saw a script that iterated on the log groups).

Incorrect. Export to S3 could reduce the storage costs of CloudWatch Logs, but o S3 ALSO has storage costs (although potentially lower with lifecycle policies), and 'excluding original log groups' would also exclude logs FUTUROS received, unless reconfigured — this is a more complex, manual and unique migration rather than a continuous automatic retention policy; setting up retention directly in the log groups is the simplest and most designed mechanism for this purpose.

Incorrect. Reducing log verbosity reduces volume FUTURO of logs, but does not treat terabytes of old log data already accumulated in CloudWatch Logs — and reduce log levels has the trade-off to reduce clearance visibility to TODOS periods, not only old data; retention policies specifically eliminate data ANTIGOS preserving recent detailed logs.

Incorrect. Migrating log storage to OpenSearch Service is a significant architectural change (different intake pipeline, different query interface) that introduces SEUS INDIVIDUAL infrastructure costs (OpenSearch computer/domain storage) — does not directly address 'reducing storage costs from CloudWatch Logs' saw a change in configuration, and may not be more economical in general.

saa-avc-196.text: A company uses AWS Step Functions Standard Workflows to orchestrate a high volume and short-duration data processing pipeline, invoked millions of times a day, with each execution ending in less than a few seconds (e.g. transformation/validation by event triggered by requests for API). They realize that the costs of Step Functions (in the Standard Workflows) have become a significant expense given the volume of MILHIONES of daily and short executions, even though for this specific workflow, resources of the Standard Workflows as a retention of execution history of up to 90 days or semantics of execution exactly-once.
options: Change this workflow to AWS Step Functions Express Workflow
Reduce the number of states in Standard Workflow to minimize state transition costs
Replace Step Functions completely by direct invocations Lambda-for-Lambda, removing the orchestration layer
Group multiple events before triggering a single execution of Step Functions Standard Workflow, to reduce the total number of executions
saa-avc-196.explanation: Correct. Express Workflows are precised based on the NUMBER OF EXECUTIONS, their DURATION and memory consumption (similar to the model of precification of the Lambda), instead of by transition of status as in Standard Workflows — for workflows of ALTO VOLUME and CURTA DURATION (millions of short runs), Express Workflows are significantly more economical; the trade-off is execution 'at-last-once' (instead of 'exactly-once' of the Standard) and retention of shorter execution history (based on CloudWatch Logs, not in the complete history of the console of Step Functions) — acceptable for this case of use of high volume and short duration that does not depend on these specific guarantees of the Standard.
saa-avc-196.hint: Workflow has millions of short runs per day and does not depend on exact-once guarantees or long-term execution history — think of what kind of Step Functions has a precision model based on execution/duration instead of by state transition.
optionRationales: Correct. Express Workflows are precised based on the NUMBER OF EXECUTIONS, their DURATION and memory consumption (similar to the model of precification of the Lambda), instead of by transition of status as in Standard Workflows — for workflows of ALTO VOLUME and CURTA DURATION (millions of short runs), Express Workflows are significantly more economical; the trade-off is execution 'at-last-once' (instead of 'exactly-once' of the Standard) and retention of shorter execution history (based on CloudWatch Logs, not in the complete history of the console of Step Functions) — acceptable for this case of use of high volume and short duration that does not depend on these specific guarantees of the Standard.

Incorrect. Remove Step Functions would completely eliminate orchestration costs, but also remove the BENEFITS from using the Step Functions (visual definition of workflow, integrated error/retries treatment, state management) — this is a much more invasive architectural change than simply changing the TIPO of workflow within the Step Functions, which directly deals with the cost problem per state transition to this execution profile.

Incorrect. Reducing the number of states could reduce the cost per execution a little (less transitions = lower cost per execution under the standard's transitional precision), but it does not fundamentally change the MODELO PRECIFICATION — For millions of daily executions, the precision model based on the execution of the Express Workflows is fundamentally more appropriate, regardless of how many states remain, without requiring a redesign of the logic of the workflow.

Incorrect. Batching could reduce the number of runs, but introduces LATENCY (waiting to accumulate a batch) for workflows described as ending 'in less than a few seconds' per event (i.e., event processing is desired) — and adds complexity to the batch division logic within the workflow; moving to Express Workflows addresses the cost problem directly without changing the execution model per event.

saa-avc-197.text: A company stores user-generated content (photos and documents) in a Amazon S3. The access pattern of each object is unpredictable: some objects are accessed intensely in the first days and then never again, while others often remain accessed for months — there is no reliable correlation between the age of the object and its access frequency. The architecture team wants to automatically optimize storage costs based on the access pattern REAL of each object over time, without defining age-based life-cycle rules and without introducing recovery rates for objects that are accessed again.
options: Store all items in S3 One Zone-IA to reduce costs, given the high volume of data.
Configure a life cycle rule of S3 which transits the objects to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and for S3 Glacier after 90 days.

Store objects in class Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which automatically moves each object between access levels (Frequently, Infrequently and, optionally, Archive Instant Access) based on the observed access pattern, without recovery rates between frequent and infrequently access levels.
Store all objects directly in S3 Standard-IA since upload, since its storage cost per GB is lower than that of S3 Standard.
saa-avc-197.explanation: Correct. S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors the access patterns of each object individually and moves it automatically between access levels (without performance impact and no recovery rate between Frequent and Infrequent Access), charging only a small rate of monitoring per object. This resolves exactly the scenario of unpredictable and uncorrelated access patterns with the age of the object, eliminating the need for age-based life-cycle rules.
saa-avc-197.hint: Think of what mechanism the S3 monitors the actual access behavior of each object, instead of assuming that age predicts the frequency of use.
optionRationales: Correct. S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors the access patterns of each object individually and moves it automatically between access levels (without performance impact and no recovery rate between Frequent and Infrequent Access), charging only a small rate of monitoring per object. This resolves exactly the scenario of unpredictable and uncorrelated access patterns with the age of the object, eliminating the need for age-based life-cycle rules.

Incorrect. Age-based life-cycle rules presuppose a correlation between age and access frequency (older objects would be less accessed). The scenario explicitly states that this correlation does NOT exist — an object can remain popular for months (generating AI recovery rates) or become cold immediately (staying in Standard without need until the 30 This violates the optimization requirement based on actual access pattern, not age.

Incorrect. S3 Standard-IA has lower storage cost, but charges a recovery rate per GB accessed. For the subset of objects that often remain accessed (as described in the scenario), these recovery rates can make the total cost greater than keeping them in S3 Standard. Apply Standard-IA uniformly to a data set with mixed and unpredictable access patterns risks increasing total cost.

Incorrect. S3 One Zone-IA reduces the storage cost by storing data in a single Availability Zone (with durability trade-off), but does not solve the optimization based on the default of ACESSO described in the scenario – in addition, it also charges recovery fees like Standard-IA, which would penalize frequently accessed objects.

saa-avc-198.text: A company operates several bodies of the Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL and Amazon Aurora MySQL using instance classes based on Intel processors (db.m5 and db.r5). FinOps team wants to reduce database computing cost SEM change the engine, the bank version, the connection drivers or the application code, migrating to a family of instances recognized for offering better price-performance ratio for compatible workloads. Applications use standard PostgreSQL/MySQL drivers, without extensions dependent on processor architecture.
options: Enable Amazon RDS Performance Insights to identify and optimize slow queries, indirectly reducing the need for computational resources.
Migrate instances RDS/Aurora for equivalent classes based on AWS Graviton (e.g. db.m5 → db.m6g, db.r5 → db.r6g), which offer better price-performance ratio for the same database engines.
Migrate databases to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2, which is always more economical than provided instances.
Purchase Reserved Instances of the RDS for the m5/r5 classes currently in use.
saa-avc-198.explanation: Right. RDS/Aurora based on AWS Graviton (db.*6(g) offer up to ~20% best price-performance ratio compared to Intel-based equivalent classes (m5/r5) for the same engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Aurora), without requiring changes to the engine version, application code or connection drivers for standard workloads — a simple change in instance class in a maintenance window.
saa-avc-198.hint: Consider which instance class change, without changing engine or application, is widely recognized for improving the price-performance ratio in managed databases.
optionRationales: Right. RDS/Aurora based on AWS Graviton (db.*6(g) offer up to ~20% best price-performance ratio compared to Intel-based equivalent classes (m5/r5) for the same engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Aurora), without requiring changes to the engine version, application code or connection drivers for standard workloads — a simple change in instance class in a maintenance window.

Incorrect. Aurora Serverless v2 is more economical for VARIABLE or intermittent workloads, but for STAFF and continuously used workloads (as suggested by the use of m5/r5), discounted instances may be more economical than the cost by ACU of Serverless v2. To state that it is 'always' more economical is an incorrect generalization, and this option does not directly respond to the request to change to a family of instances with better performance-price.

Incorrect. Adjust Slow Queries PODE reducing resource consumption, but it is an optimization in the level of application/query with uncertain economy and dependent on workload — does not directly correspond to the request to 'change to a family of instances with better price-performance', which is a change of direct infrastructure (Graviton). It is a valid but complementary optimization and of different nature.

Incorrect. Reserved Instances offer discount on the invoice, but do not change the relationship PRICE-DESEMPENHO The scenario specifically calls for a change to a family with better performance-price (Graviton), which is a complementary (and combinable) optimization to Reserved Instances, but approaches a different cost lever.

saa-avc-199.text: An account AWS has accumulated, over several years, a large number of snapshots of the Amazon EBS (many from automated backup processes whose retention has never been configured) and volumes EBS which are no longer attached to any body EC2 (leftovers of closed instances without 'Delete on Termination' enabled, or disconnected and forgotten volumes). These resources contribute significantly to the storage invoice EBS, but the team is not sure which snapshots/volumes are still needed for recovery. The company wants a SYSTEMATIC approach to reduce this cost and identify candidates for cleaning, without the risk of excluding resources that are still needed.
options: Use the 'Underused' check Amazon EBS Volumes AWS Trusted Advisor to identify non-attached volumes as candidates for cleaning, and implement a policy of Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) or AWS Backup to manage snapshot retention automatically from now on, reviewing old snapshots against this policy before deleting them.
Write a script that immediately deletes all snapshots EBS with more than 30 days and all volumes EBS Unattached.
Move all snapshots EBS for the Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive to Reduce Storage Cost.
Convert all volumes EBS not attached in snapshots, since snapshots are cheaper than volumes.
saa-avc-199.explanation: Right. Trusted Advisor (identification of unattached volumes) with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (automated snapshot retention and deletion policies) addresses both accumulation EXISTENTE (by reviewing against a pre-exclusion retention policy) how long it prevents accumulation FUTURO (by automatic retention-based exclusion) — a systematic and policy-oriented approach instead of ad hoc exclusion.
saa-avc-199.hint: Think of a combination of an underutilized resource identification tool with a policy-based snapshot life cycle automation tool.
optionRationales: Right. Trusted Advisor (identification of unattached volumes) with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (automated snapshot retention and deletion policies) addresses both accumulation EXISTENTE (by reviewing against a pre-exclusion retention policy) how long it prevents accumulation FUTURO (by automatic retention-based exclusion) — a systematic and policy-oriented approach instead of ad hoc exclusion.

Incorrect. Exclude indiscriminately based only on age/attachment status, SEM first to establish which retention is really necessary (for example compliance requirements may require keeping certain snapshots for years), risks EXCLUSSION PERMANENTE of resources still needed for recovery — exactly the risk the scenario requires to avoid..

Incorrect. EBS are not objects S3 standard that the customer can 'move' directly between storage classes S3 via life cycle policies — they are stored incrementally in a system managed by AWS, without direct customer access to storage class transition. This operation is not available.

Incorrect. Although a snapshot of a volume is usually cheaper to store than the volume itself (snapshots are incremental and tablets), simply converting volumes into snapshots without first determining whether the data are NECESSARY does not solve the central question of 'what are candidates for cleaning' — and does not establish the systematic retention policy necessary to prevent the same accumulation problem from recurring, now with snapshots instead of volumes.

saa-avc-200.text: A company has a function AWS Lambda performing an intensive data transformation in CPU and memory. The team knows that the billed duration of Lambda depends on the memory configuration (more memory = more CPU proportional = possibly faster execution, which can result in lower OR higher cost depending on the relationship between memory increase and duration reduction PARA ESSA SPECIFIC FUNCTION), but you don't know what the Optimum memory configuration minimizes the cost (or balance cost and speed) for this function. Manually testing each memory configuration by repeatedly implanting and invoking would be extremely laborious.
options: Enable memory recommendations from AWS Compute Optimizer for the Lambda and apply the suggested memory size.
Configure the function memory to the maximum allowed value (10.240 MB) to ensure the fastest possible execution and thus the lowest cost based on duration.
Convert function to use Provided Competition, ensuring consistent performance regardless of memory configuration.

Use the open-source tool AWS Lambda Power Tuning (a state machine of the AWS Step Functions available in AWS Serverless Application Repository), which runs the function automatically in several memory settings and generates a view of the cost-x-duration ratio to identify the configuration that minimizes the cost (or another chosen goal)).
saa-avc-200.explanation: Correct. AWS Lambda Power Tuning automates the function test in a range of memory settings, running it multiple times in each configuration and producing a cost x duration trade-off curve, identifying the memory configuration that minimizes the cost (or optimizes for speed or balance) — exactly automating the manual and labor test described in the scenario.
saa-avc-200.hint: Think of a tool that empirically tests various memory settings and maps the cost versus duration curve, instead of based only on history or assumptions.
optionRationales: Correct. AWS Lambda Power Tuning automates the function test in a range of memory settings, running it multiple times in each configuration and producing a cost x duration trade-off curve, identifying the memory configuration that minimizes the cost (or optimizes for speed or balance) — exactly automating the manual and labor test described in the scenario.

Incorrect. Computer Optimizer provides memory recommendations for the Lambda based on historical metrics of use of the CloudWatch (a valid and complementary tool), but it analyzes the history of invocations PASSADAS to suggest UMA Recommendation, instead of empirically testing a FAIXA of configurations to map the entire trade-off curve cost/duration, as does the Lambda Power Tuning — to explore the entire configuration space, Power Tuning is the most direct approach to this scenario.

Incorrect. Maximizing memory maximizes allocation of CPU and probably minimizes the duration, but the CUSTO is duration × memory (GB-(seconds) — a function that performs twice as fast with 4x plus memory can actually cost approximately the DOBRO, no less. 'Fast execution' does not amount to 'less cost'; the relationship is specific to each workload and must be determined empirically, not assumed when maximizing memory..

Incorrect. Provided Competition solves the latency of COLD START maintaining pre-initialized execution environments, but does not alter the relationship between MEMORY ALLOCATION and DURATION/CUSTO EXECUTION of function processing — is an orthogonal concern (cold start) to memory optimization-vs-cost described in the scenario, and adds its own extra cost.

saa-avc-201.text: A company owns a Amazon S3 with millions of objects accumulated over the years, without any life cycle policy configured today. SUSPEITA that many older objects are rarely accessed and could be moved to a cheaper storage class, but wants EVIDENCES BASEADAS EM DADOS about the actual access patterns (as the age of the objects relates to the access frequency)) ANTES to define rules of transition of life cycle, in order to avoid defining very aggressive transition times (generating recovery rates for objects still actively used) or very conservative (losing economic opportunities)).
options: Enable S3 Storage Class Analysis in the Bucket (optionally limited to specific prefixes or tags), which observes access patterns over time and generates reports showing how the age of the objects correlates with the access frequency for the analyzed dataset.
Enable directly the S3 Intelligent-Tiering, eliminating the need for analysis of access patterns.
Use AWS Cost Explorer to view the storage costs of the S3 segmented by storage class over time.
Enable S3 Server Access Logging and analyze the logs with Amazon Athena to determine access patterns.
saa-avc-201.explanation: Correct. S3 Storage Class Analysis observes access patterns over a period (usually 30+ days) and provides reports/views showing where the objects of this specific bucket move from 'frequently accessed' to 'rarely accessed', providing the data-oriented basis for defining life-cycle rules with appropriate time frames, instead of divining.
saa-avc-201.hint: Think of a functionality of S3 specifically designed to observe and report the relationship between age of objects and frequency of access, before defining life cycle transitions.
optionRationales: Correct. S3 Storage Class Analysis observes access patterns over a period (usually 30+ days) and provides reports/views showing where the objects of this specific bucket move from 'frequently accessed' to 'rarely accessed', providing the data-oriented basis for defining life-cycle rules with appropriate time frames, instead of divining.

Incorrect. The access logs of the S3 contain data at the request level that PODERIAM be analyzed, but this requires significant manual effort (enable logging, wait for data accumulation, develop queries/views in the Athena to correlate the age of the object with access frequency in millions of objects). S3 Storage Class Analysis provides this specific age-vs-frequency analysis as a native and ready report, without the need to develop custom queries.

Incorrect. Intelligent-Tiering is a valid alternative that avoids the need to analyze patterns previously (it automatically adapts), but the scenario specifically asks for a tool to collect EVIDES before defining rules of CICLO OF VIDA (implying that the team wants traditional transitions, possibly for specific architectural reasons. The Storage Class Analysis is the tool designed for INFORMAR life-cycle rule decisions, which is what is being requested.

Incorrect. Cost Explorer shows trends in CUSTO by storage class (used to accompany the IMPACTO of changes already made), but does not show access pattern data at the level of OBJETO (which objects/prefixes/ities are accessed at what frequency) necessary to determine the appropriate life-cycle transition thresholds before making changes — is a cost report tool, not access pattern analysis.

saa-avc-202.text: A company operates 10 independent microservices, each behind its own Application Load Balancer dedicated, all in the same VPC and attending traffic to the same domain (different paths or subdomains per service, ex.: api.example.com/orders, api.example.com/stock). ALB generates its own collection per hour, in addition to the collections by Load Balancer Capacity Unit (LCU). The team wants to reduce the number of load balancers (and associated hourly charges), keeping the traffic router for the correct target group of each microservice based on the route or host of the request.
options: Replace 10 ALBs by a single Network Load Balancer with routing at the level of TCP.

Consolidate microservices behind a SINGLE Application Load Balancer, using router rules based on path and/or host (lister rules) to direct traffic to the corresponding target group of each microservice.
Use weighted routing (weighted routing) of Amazon Route 53 to distribute traffic between 10 Existing ALBs.
Place the Amazon CloudFront in front of the 10 ALBs and configure the CloudFront to route based on road patterns for each ALB of origin.
saa-avc-202.explanation: Right. ALB support routing for different target groups based on path patterns, Host headers, headers, etc., allowing MULTIPLES microservices to share a SINGLE ALB (and their hourly collection), each with its own target group and independent health checks — significantly reducing the number of required ALBs and associated costs, maintaining route routing/hosting required.
saa-avc-202.hint: Think of a Layer Routing feature 7 which allows a single load balancer direct requests to different target groups based on the content of the request.
optionRationales: Right. ALB support routing for different target groups based on path patterns, Host headers, headers, etc., allowing MULTIPLES microservices to share a SINGLE ALB (and their hourly collection), each with its own target group and independent health checks — significantly reducing the number of required ALBs and associated costs, maintaining route routing/hosting required.

Incorrect. Load Balancer operates in the Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and DO NOT support route-based or host-based routing rules 7/HTTP) to direct traffic to different target groups based on URL or in the Host header. This would not allow you to route different microservices based on path/host as required; the ALB (Layer 7) is the appropriate type for this route requirement.

Incorrect. Weighted routing distributes traffic PROPORCIONALMENTE between multiple endpoints (e.g. for canary implantations or load distribution between IDENTICAL backends), but not REDUZ the number of ALBs (all 10 would continue to exist and generate collections) — and is not designed to ROTEAR Requirements DIFERENTES for SERVICES DIFERENTES based on path/host (this is content based router, not weighted distribution)).

Incorrect. Although the CloudFront can route to different origins based on path patterns (cache behaviors), this would still require that all 10 ALBs EXISTISSEM and continue to generate their hourly collections as origins of CloudFront — add a layer of CDN without reducing the number/cost of underlying ALBs, which is the stated objective; consolidate into a single ALB with listener rules directly reduces the number of ALBs.

saa-avc-203.text: A company uses the Amazon EFS (General Purpose performance mode) as shared file system, accessed by an application in multiple instances EC2. The analysis shows that most files, once recorded, are rarely accessed again after about 30 The team wants to reduce storage costs of the EFS for most rarely accessed files, SEM identify/move files manually, while files that are still accessed (even rarely) remain available through MESMA File system interface without a separate recovery process.
options: Provide a second file system EFS, smaller, specifically for rarely accessed files, making the application record on the appropriate file system based on expected access frequency.
Move rarely accessed files to Amazon S3 Glacier and mount the S3 via a file system driver based on FUSE when necessary.
Enable EFS Lifecycle Management with a policy to transition files to storage class EFS Access infrequent (EFS-IA) after a period configured without access (ex.: 30 days).
Change File System EFS General Purpose performance mode for Max I/O.
saa-avc-203.explanation: Correct. EFS Lifecycle Management automatically moves files that have not been accessed during the period configured for class EFS-IA, lower cost, while the files remain in MESMO file system namespace/interface (transparently accessible, with a GB access rate for AI files, but without a separate 'restore' process like Glacier) — meeting exactly the access pattern described without manual file management.
saa-avc-203.hint: Think of a resource of the EFS which automatically moves files to a cheaper storage class based on access history, keeping them in the same namespace.
optionRationales: Correct. EFS Lifecycle Management automatically moves files that have not been accessed during the period configured for class EFS-IA, lower cost, while the files remain in MESMO file system namespace/interface (transparently accessible, with a GB access rate for AI files, but without a separate 'restore' process like Glacier) — meeting exactly the access pattern described without manual file management.

Incorrect. This would require identifying and migrating individual files PARA FORA of the EFS for the S3 (a manual/customs migration process), and S3 Glacier requires an explicit process of RESTORE before the files become accessible (hour rate) — contradicting the requirement that rarely accessed files remain available by MESMA interface, without separate recovery process; or EFS-IA keeps the files in the namespace of EFS with standard access (only slightly slower)).

Incorrect. Max I/O mode is a configuration of PERFORMANCE (optimized for higher levels of throughput/IOPS aggregates, with latency by slightly larger operation), not an optimization of CUSTO OF ARMAZENAMENTO — does not move data to a cheaper storage layer and is not related to the cost reduction goal based on access pattern described.

Incorrect. This would require that the APPLICATION be modified to determine, MOMENTO GRAVATION, which file system to use based on an access frequency PREVISTA (this scenario suggests not to be known reliably in advance, since the access pattern emerges over time). EFS Lifecycle Management automatically treats this transition based on access OBSERVADO over time, without requiring the application to provide access patterns at the time of recording.

saa-avc-204.text: A company has several instances EC2 running application code that makes POLLING CONTINUED in one API external, database table or pocket S3 every few seconds, 24 hours a day, looking for new items to process — even if new items arrive sporadically (sometimes with interval hours). EC2 they run all the time mainly to perform this polling, consuming computational resources (and generating costs of EC2) even for long periods without anything to process. The team wants to eliminate the cost of computing dedicated to continuous polling, processing items only when they actually arrive.
options: Use AWS Auto Scaling to reduce instances EC2 for a minimum of 1 during periods of lower demand.

Redesign the architecture for an event-oriented model: configure the source (e.g. event notifications from S3, DynamoDB Streams, or an scheduled/disposed mechanism for external APIs) to send events to a row Amazon SQS (or shoot directly at AWS Lambda), and use a function AWS Lambda driven by the queue/event/stream to perform the processing.
Move Polling Logic to an Scheduled Job within the Database RDS (using pg_cron or similar) to remove it from the instances EC2.
Replace instances EC2 by smaller/ cheaper instance types that continue to perform the same polling logic continuously.
saa-avc-204.explanation: That redesign eliminates the need for instances EC2 in continuous execution dedicated to polling; AWS Lambda is invoked (and charged) only when there is in fact an item to process, eliminating computing costs during idle periods between sporadic arrivals of items — meeting directly the goal of 'paying only when there is work'.'.
saa-avc-204.hint: Think of an architecture in which processing is invoked (and charged) only when a real event occurs, completely eliminating idle computing between events.
optionRationales: That redesign eliminates the need for instances EC2 in continuous execution dedicated to polling; AWS Lambda is invoked (and charged) only when there is in fact an item to process, eliminating computing costs during idle periods between sporadic arrivals of items — meeting directly the goal of 'paying only when there is work'.'.

Incorrect.
